questions.q: What is the key difference between an IAM role and an IAM user?
options: A role has no long-term credentials — it issues temporary, auto-expiring credentials when assumed; a user has long-lived credentials
A role can only be used by humans, never by AWS services
A user can be assumed by a service; a role cannot
There is no functional difference between the two
questions.explain: IAM users carry long-term credentials (passwords or access keys) until rotated. IAM roles have no standing credentials — assuming a role issues temporary credentials that expire automatically.

questions.q: What does a role's trust policy define?
options: Who or what is allowed to assume the role
What actions the role can perform once assumed
Which S3 storage class the role's data uses
The expiration time of the AWS account
questions.explain: The trust policy names the principal(s) permitted to assume the role. The separate permissions policy defines what the role can actually do once assumed.

questions.q: What is a 'service principal' in a trust policy?
options: A special identifier representing an AWS service, like glue.amazonaws.com, that is trusted to assume a role
The IAM user who created the role
The root account owner of the AWS account
A wildcard that allows any AWS service to assume any role
questions.explain: A service principal (e.g. glue.amazonaws.com or lambda.amazonaws.com) identifies a specific AWS service as the trusted entity in a role's trust policy.

questions.q: If a Glue job's role has a trust policy naming lambda.amazonaws.com instead of glue.amazonaws.com, what happens when Glue tries to assume that role?
options: The assumption is rejected, because Glue's principal doesn't match the trusted principal in the trust policy
Glue is granted access anyway since trust policies are optional
AWS automatically corrects the principal to glue.amazonaws.com
The job runs with full administrator access as a fallback
questions.explain: The trust policy strictly controls which principal may call sts:AssumeRole on that role — a mismatched principal results in the assumption being denied.

questions.q: Why are long-lived IAM user access keys considered a worse default than roles for AWS services?
options: A leaked access key remains valid until manually rotated, while a role's temporary credentials expire automatically and are never stored persistently
Access keys are more expensive to use than roles
AWS services are technically incapable of using access keys
Access keys provide broader permissions than any role can have
questions.explain: A leaked long-lived access key is a standing liability until someone notices and rotates it. A role's temporary credentials expire on their own (typically within an hour) and are never stored persistently.
